newsitem.title: USA: US senator raps Babbitt over Interior budget plan.
newsitem.headline: US senator raps Babbitt over Interior budget plan.

text.p: The chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Tuesday criticized the Clinton administration's proposed fiscal 1998 Interior Department budget as too costly, with mixed-up priorities.

"Other federal departments are taking hits in the overall government downsizing, but yours seems to be soaking up all the gravy," Chairman Frank Murkowski, Alaska Republican, told Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt at a hearing.

Murkowksi complained the White House was seeking a $462 million, or 6.6 percent, increase for next fiscal year's Interior budget over the 1997 level. But the Bureau of Land Management and the Minerals Management Service, which generate revenue, would get only small increases.
Babbitt responded the proposed budget still was below 1993 levels, and said his department had borne a disproportionate share of earlier budget cuts.
He also said more budget priorities could be met with initiatives such as raising fees charged to national parks concessionaires and imposing royalties on hardrock minerals from federal lands.

"Hardrock minerals are the last asset that I know of that the federal government is giving away free entirely outside the market system. It is simply outrageous to perpetuate this giveaway," Babbitt said.

Babbitt said he believed the net smelter royalty could be imposed without authorizing legislation, but Idaho Republican Larry Craig pressed him for more information on the plan which would generate some $778 million.
"This is not something that you snap your fingers and let the IRS (Internal Revenue Service) run loose on," Craig said.

Also at the hearing, Babbitt said proposed controlled forest burns to reduce the threat of major fires could pose a problem in western states with the Environmental Protection Agency's plan to tighten air quality standards against soot and smog.

"It's a serious issue and we are going to look at it very carefully," Babbitt said. But he said he thought the EPA, the Forest Service and the Interior Department felt the control burns could be conducted in compliance with the stricter air standards.
